children: Copper briefly rose above $12,000 a metric ton on Thursday after two days of steep selloffs, as Asian shares recovered some ground and the latest US tariff proposals appeared less damaging than feared.
on the London Metal Exchange rose 2.65% to $11,958 a metric ton as of 0335 GMT, after rising to $12,089, passing the $12,000 mark.
And the most-active copper contract (SCFv1) on the Shanghai Futures Exchange edged down 0.07% to 89,700 yuan ($13,438) a ton.

US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, following an investigation into excess industrial capacity.
The proposed duties, however, will not stack on top of those imposed in July and are unlikely to take effect until February or March.

"The recent selloff in risk assets has been driven mainly by concerns over AI and macroeconomic headwinds, with negative free cash flows and expectations of hawkish monetary policy dominating market sentiment," analysts at Chinese broker Jinrui Futures said in a note, adding that US tariffs had largely been priced in, with their influence on trading diminishing.
also helped to lift prices, by making the greenback-denominated metal more affordable for buyers using other currencies.
On the SHFE, aluminium (SAFv1) rose 0.64%, zinc (SZNv1) slipped 0.06%, lead (SPBv1) gained 0.39%, nickel (SNIv1) climbed 1.48% and tin (SSNv1) fell 3.57%.
